question: explain your experience with Kafka
answer:
I wrote the application-side Kafka producer and consumer code at BCBSA, tied to member, coverage and claims changes. The pattern was straightforward: a backend service processes a change, publishes an event, and a downstream consumer picks it up and applies the update on its side. That kept the receiving service current without the source service having to synchronously coordinate with every consumer on every change.

I was on the application side of this, not administration. I didn't set up the brokers, and I don't remember the retry, offset or dead-letter configuration for when a consumer failed to process something. What I can speak to directly is the producer and consumer code I wrote and the change-propagation flow it supported.

Kafka wasn't part of the stack at my other employers, so BCBSA is really the one place I can talk about it from hands-on work.

answer:

question: tell me about your multithreading experience
answer:
My clearest multithreading story is at NRG, on the dashboard's readProduct flow. It used to call out to several downstream services one after another - profile and contract data, offers, content, Vivint flags - and that added up to several seconds of load time. We parallelized those calls using CompletableFuture, and the load time dropped to around a second.

That was a deliberate, targeted fix for a specific slow flow, not a pattern we used everywhere - most of the codebase, including flows like the DOD/Vivint-eligibility check, stayed sequential and blocking. So async and parallel calls were the exception applied where it mattered, not the default coding style.

I don't have JVM-level tuning detail like thread-pool sizing or GC settings to go with that - that layer just wasn't something I worked in directly.

question: what async messaging do you use at NRG
answer:
At NRG we didn't use Kafka. The async messaging there ran on SQS with dead-letter queues, alongside scheduled and event-driven AWS mechanisms.

One concrete example I worked with: JWT issuance in one of the Lambda functions enqueues directly onto an account-mapping-processing SQS queue as part of token issuance, and that queue has its own DLQ. The visibility timeout on those queues was deliberately set higher than the Lambda timeout, so a message that fails becomes visible again for redrive after the function would have timed out. I didn't see a redrive policy or alerting threshold built on top of that DLQ mechanism -- it was more that the DLQ existed as the safety net.

Beyond that queue-based work, there was also a weekly scheduled cleanup job for Lambda versions, since a new immutable version gets published on every deploy across all the functions. That's the extent of the async messaging picture at NRG -- no Kafka, no pub/sub broker, just SQS-centered patterns plus scheduled jobs.

question: how does the human approval step work in your platform
answer:
The approval step is structural, not a prompt instruction. When the agent proposes a code change, the approve step hashes the path and content together at the moment of approval. Then when the change is actually applied, it checks that hash again — if either the path or the content changed since approval, it refuses to proceed. I have tests proving both a content substitution and a path substitution after approval are independently rejected.

The other half of it is on the authority side: the approve and reject functions are plain Python functions that are never listed in the tool schemas and never reachable through the model's dispatch path. So it's not that the model is told not to self-approve — there's literally no code path for it to call approve on its own work. I verified that with an exact set-membership check, not just a substring check, plus a check that the dispatch function can't reach it, and separately proved that if the model puts an "approval" field in its own output, it's ignored.

It's also fail-closed: if the approval prompt hits a non-interactive input and gets an EOF, it defaults to reject rather than crashing or defaulting to approve, and I verified that with a test and reproduced it live. I did run a real browser session where a human clicked approve and the full pipeline — apply, compile, test, commit, deploy, verify — ran to completion.

One honest gap: it's a single global approval registry, so it's built for one run at a time, not concurrent multi-user approvals, and that's documented rather than hidden.

question: how does RAG work in this Standing Interview
answer:
For this Standing Interview, I built retrieval over my own private notes so answers are grounded in what I actually did rather than made up on the spot. The notes get chunked and embedded with a local embedding model, fastembed running BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, so there's no API key needed for that part. I index them into a local JSON store with numpy doing cosine similarity, no external vector database, since the scale here doesn't call for one.

On top of that there's a labeled retrieval evaluation, so I can measure Recall@K and MRR against a small dataset rather than just eyeballing whether answers look right. Indexing is incremental too, based on content hashes, so re-indexing after a small change doesn't re-embed everything that hasn't changed.

When a question comes in, it gets embedded and compared against that index to pull the most relevant chunks, and the answer gets built from those chunks with a grounding check and a decline gate before anything reaches you, so if the notes don't support an answer I say so instead of guessing. What I haven't added yet is reranking or hybrid keyword-plus-vector search, since with a corpus this size the plain cosine retrieval has been enough.

question: tell me about a production incident you handled
answer:

question: what REST API work have you done
answer:
Most of my REST API work has been at NRG, in the classic Spring Boot aggregator and in the Lambda layer.

In the aggregator, I built and maintained REST controllers using RequestMapping and GetMapping, backing endpoints like lead creation, usage history, and preferences. A typical flow I worked in built a downstream URL through positional templating, called the downstream service synchronously through a named RestTemplate bean, parsed the response, and sometimes made a second sequential call before assembling the final response back to the client. That pattern was strictly sequential in most flows I touched, though on the dashboard specifically the team parallelized one call that fanned out to several downstream services, which brought the load time down noticeably.

In 2025 I also wrote REST APIs in the Lambda layer, each function backed by its own OpenAPI definition and tested locally against dev before anything went further. That layer is REST only, no GraphQL there, covering things like profile lookup, account lookup, and validation-style endpoints.

Separately, in 2024, I worked on migrating some flows that had been GraphQL over to REST in that same aggregator, so I've touched both the REST-only Lambda side and the REST-plus-GraphQL side of the aggregator.

question: walk me through how you handled concurrency at NRG
answer:
At NRG, the main concurrency story I can point to is the dashboard's readProduct call. It used to fan out sequentially to several downstream services — SAP-backed profile and contract data, offers, content, Vivint flags — calling them one after another. We parallelized that using CompletableFuture, and load time dropped from several seconds down to roughly a second. I don't have an independently measured before/after number, just that commit-level change and the reported improvement.

That said, I want to be accurate about scope: this was the exception, not the pattern. I looked at other flows in that codebase, like the DOD/Vivint-eligibility flow, and those stayed strictly sequential and blocking. So async and parallel patterns weren't a default coding style there — they got applied selectively to specific slow flows where fan-out latency was actually a problem, and readProduct was the clear case of that.

Beyond that call, I don't have a broader reactive or async story for NRG — there was no WebClient or reactive-stack pattern running through the codebase, and no heap or JVM-level tuning work tied to concurrency either. It really came down to identifying one slow, multi-call flow and parallelizing it directly.
